titolo: India Gave English an Expiry Date. Why Is It Still Around?
descrizione:
In 1950, India's constitution gave English an expiry date: January 26, 1965. Hindi was supposed to take over. Instead, the deadline brought riots, about 70 deaths by the official count, and a law that keeps English alive for as long as the non-Hindi states want it. This video follows the story from the East India Company to Macaulay, Gandhi, Nehru and the Tamil protests.

Why could India not get rid of the language of its old rulers? The answer is less about business and more about Tamil, about a country with no single mother tongue, and about a language that belongs to nobody. Watch to the end for the surprising numbers on who really speaks English in India today.

scene.testo: India set a deadline to drop English: January 26, 1965. Riots, about 70 dead, and a law that keeps it forever. A language that would not leave.
So why could India never get rid of English?
In 1950, India's constitution said English could stay for 15 years. After that, Hindi would take over national government. The deadline was January 26, 1965.
Parliament could keep English longer, but the plan was clear: Hindi first. Then the day arrived, and the south exploded.
Protests swept Madras state. In a few weeks, about 70 people died, by the government's own count.
Less than three years later, Parliament passed a law keeping English for as long as non-Hindi states want it. It is still there today.
Other former colonies faced the same question. In the Philippines, Indonesia and Brazil, the colonial language faded or won only after a long fight.
India is the reverse. It tried to drop English and failed. Business is only part of the reason.
The real reason has less to do with English than with Tamil. To see why, we go back 400 years.
In 1600, Queen Elizabeth the First gave London merchants the sole English right to trade with Asia. They became the East India Company.

eventi.descrizione: 16th-century English queen, red hair, ruff collar, crown

scene.testo: For a long time they were mostly traders. Then in 1757, they won the Battle of Plassey.
Plassey put the company on the road to ruling Bengal, one of the richest regions in the world at the time.
But when the company started governing, it did not use English. It kept Persian, the language of the Mughal emperors.
The big turning point came in 1835. Since 1813, the company had to spend 100,000 rupees a year on education, mostly on Sanskrit and Arabic.
Should that money switch to English? The man who settled the fight was Thomas Babington Macaulay.

eventi.descrizione: 19th-century British politician and historian, dark coat, high collar

scene.testo: Macaulay believed one shelf of a good European library was worth all the literature of India and Arabia together. He wrote it down.
He did not want to teach English to everyone. There was no money for that.
He wanted a small class of interpreters between rulers and millions: Indian in blood and color, English in tastes, opinions, morals and intellect.
Governor-General Lord William Bentinck sided with him. From then on, education money went to English, and soon English replaced Persian in the top courts.

eventi.descrizione: British Governor-General of India, 1830s uniform, grey hair

scene.testo: In 1857, universities opened in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras. From then on, higher education in India meant English.
And the best students turned English against the British. In 1885, the Indian National Congress met for the first time in Bombay.
Delegates came from all over India with no shared mother tongue, so the meeting ran in English. It became the language of arguing for freedom.
Gandhi hated that. In 1909, he wrote that giving millions a knowledge of English was to enslave them.

eventi.descrizione: Indian leader, round glasses, white shawl, bald

scene.testo: His answer was Hindustani, the everyday speech of the north between Hindi and Urdu, writable in either script. He called it a sweet mingling.
But much of India did not speak it at all, especially the south. Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to a totally different family.
They are Dravidian languages. Hindi is Indo-European, a distant cousin of English. Tamil is related to neither.
The south had its first big fight before independence. In 1937, Congress won the election in Madras, the big province covering most of the south.
Its chief minister wanted every young person to learn the most widely spoken language in India. In 1938, he made Hindi compulsory in 125 secondary schools.
Many Tamils saw it as the north placing itself above them. Led by reformer Periyar, protests followed.

eventi.descrizione: Tamil social reformer, white beard, bald, wearing dark glasses

scene.testo: More than 1,100 people were arrested and two protesters died in custody. In 1939, the British governor made Hindi optional again.
So the Tamil fight against Hindi is older than independent India. Then came 1947: independence and partition.
Historian Ramachandra Guha says partition more or less killed the case for Hindustani. The push became Hindi alone, in Devanagari script, with Sanskrit words replacing Persian and Arabic ones.

eventi.descrizione: Indian historian, grey hair, glasses, kurta

scene.testo: Writing the constitution, language was one of the hardest fights. Frank Anthony said English is an Indian language.

eventi.descrizione: Anglo-Indian member of the Constituent Assembly, suit, mustache

scene.testo: Maulana Azad warned that north and south had only been united through English.

eventi.descrizione: Indian scholar and leader, white beard, cap, round glasses

scene.testo: On September 14, 1949, they struck a compromise. Hindi in Devanagari would be the union's official language, with English alongside for 15 more years.
Notice the word official. Strictly speaking, India has no national language. In 2010, the Gujarat High Court said nothing ever declared Hindi one.
Meanwhile language was redrawing the map. Tamil and Telugu speakers shared one big Madras state.
In 1952, Potti Sriramulu went on hunger strike for a Telugu state. He died after 58 days.

eventi.descrizione: Telugu activist, thin, white dhoti, gandhian

scene.testo: Four days later, Prime Minister Nehru announced the state of Andhra. In 1956, India redrew its borders largely along language lines.

eventi.descrizione: India's first prime minister, white cap, sherwani with rose

scene.testo: The new map had 14 states and six union territories, each shaped by the language its people spoke.
As 1965 neared, non-Hindi states got nervous. In 1959, Nehru told Parliament English would stay as long as people needed it.
He said the choice would belong not to Hindi speakers but to non-Hindi speakers. In 1963, that became law, sort of.
The act said English may continue. Southern critics said may was no guarantee. Nehru called it absurd to say may also meant may not.
Then in May 1964, Nehru died. The man who made the promise was gone, eight months before the deadline.
His successor, Lal Bahadur Shastri, said keeping English forever seemed to him a deeply humiliating proposition.

eventi.descrizione: Indian prime minister, small man, white cap, dhoti and kurta

scene.testo: In Madras, the Tamil party DMK declared January 26 a day of mourning. On the 25th, students clashed with Congress workers in Madurai.
The clash became a riot. On the 26th, 50,000 students marched through Madras, and it spread from there.
Several protesters took their own lives. Police and paramilitary forces fired on crowds, and rioters killed two policemen.
After weeks of rioting, about 70 were dead by the official count. Some unofficial reports say as many as 500.
On February 11, Shastri went on All India Radio and promised to honor Nehru's word.
It took until December 1967 to write it into law. English can be dropped only if every state that has not adopted Hindi votes for it.
Both houses of Parliament must agree too. In practice, English is not going anywhere.
The protests changed Tamil politics. In 1967, the DMK swept Congress out of power in the state election.
A student protest leader beat K. Kamaraj, the Congress party president, in his home seat. Congress has not led the state since.

eventi.descrizione: Congress party president, Tamil leader, dark skin, white dhoti, mustache

scene.testo: In 1969, Madras state was renamed Tamil Nadu. Around then came the three-language formula: English, Hindi and one more Indian language.
Tamil Nadu never signed up. Its schools teach Tamil and English, and that is it.
So how many people in India really speak English? The 2011 census found just 259,678 who call it their first language.
In a country of over a billion, that is almost nothing. But add second and third language speakers, and you get about 128 million.
That is nearly twice the population of the United Kingdom, a country of about 68 million, speaking English in a land that nearly banned it.
Hindi is far bigger: about 528 million first-language speakers, though that counts related languages like Bhojpuri as Hindi.
English is still the language of India's Supreme Court. In 2024, someone asked the court to work in Hindi. The Chief Justice asked: why only Hindi?
The argument never went away. The central government calls Hindi a bridge between languages and denies forcing it on anyone.
In 2025, Tamil Nadu took the central government to the Supreme Court over school funding it says was held back for refusing Hindi.
That same year, Maharashtra made Hindi a compulsory third language for young children, then backed down after protests.
And Tamil Nadu's brand new government, elected in May 2026, says it is sticking with Tamil and English.
So English was meant to be a stopgap, yet it is still here more than 60 years after its deadline. Why do many southerners prefer it?
Because it belongs to nobody. A Tamil speaker and a Hindi speaker both have to learn it, so neither gets a head start.
The catch: English still pays whoever learns it well. One study found Indian men with fluent English earn about a third more per hour.
The language Gandhi warned would enslave India became one of the main ways Indians from opposite ends of the country talk to each other.

eventi.testo: The slave language became a bridge
